title: What drug and alcohol training must pipeline operators provide under 49 CFR Part 199?
seoTitle: PHMSA pipeline drug and alcohol training
description: 49 CFR Part 199 explained: EAP education for pipeline workers, 60 minute supervisor modules in 199.113 and 199.241, contractor coverage and training records.
shortAnswer: Under 49 CFR Part 199, pipeline and LNG operators regulated by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration must run an Employee Assistance Program that includes drug education for covered employees, give supervisors who make reasonable cause drug testing decisions one 60 minute period of training under 49 CFR 199.113, and give supervisors who make alcohol reasonable suspicion decisions at least 60 minutes of training under 49 CFR 199.241. The rules reach contractors performing covered functions.
keyTakeaways: Part 199 covers operators of facilities regulated by 49 CFR Parts 192, 193 and 195 and anyone, including contractors, who performs an operations, maintenance or emergency response function on a pipeline or LNG facility (49 CFR 199.3).
EAP education must include display and distribution of informational material, a community service hotline number and the operator's drug policy (49 CFR 199.113(b)).
Supervisors who decide on reasonable cause drug tests need one 60 minute period of training on specific, contemporaneous physical, behavioral and performance indicators (49 CFR 199.113(c)).

Supervisors who decide on reasonable suspicion alcohol tests need at least 60 minutes on physical, behavioral, speech and performance indicators, and may not conduct the breath test themselves (49 CFR 199.241 and 199.225(b)).
Drug program training records are kept for at least three years under 199.117, while alcohol program training records are kept for at least two years under 199.227.
regulator: Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), U.S. Department of Transportation, under 49 CFR Part 199 and the testing procedures in 49 CFR Part 40
appliesTo: Operators of gas, hazardous liquid and LNG facilities subject to 49 CFR Parts 192, 193 or 195
Contractors and contractor employees who perform covered operations, maintenance or emergency response functions
Supervisors who make reasonable cause drug or reasonable suspicion alcohol determinations
Covered employees located in the United States, including the Outer Continental Shelf

blocks.text: Part 199 covers pipeline operators and every person who performs a covered function for them, including contractors and their employees. Under [49 CFR 199.3](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/199.3), a covered function is "an operations, maintenance, or emergency-response function regulated by part 192, 193, or 195 of this chapter that is performed on a pipeline or on an LNG facility."

The definition of performing a covered function includes being ready or immediately available to perform it, so on call technicians count. [49 CFR 199.2](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/199.2) sets the territorial and system limits:

items: It applies only to employees located within the territory of the United States, including the Outer Continental Shelf.
It does not apply where compliance would violate the domestic laws or policies of another country.
It does not apply to covered functions on master meter systems or on pipeline systems that transport only petroleum gas or petroleum gas and air mixtures.

blocks.text: Because contractors are covered employees, an operator's program has to reach the contractor workforce that performs line locating, maintenance or emergency response. That makes contractor training evidence part of the operator's own compliance file. For the wider energy context see [energy and resources](/industries/energy-resources).

sections.heading: Where do training requirements sit in a pipeline operator's plans?

blocks.text: Operators must maintain and follow two written plans, an anti-drug plan and an alcohol misuse plan, and both must set out the education and training elements. The drug training rules sit in Subpart B and the alcohol rules in Subpart C.

items: Under 49 CFR 199.101, the anti-drug plan must contain methods and procedures for compliance with all of Part 199, "including the employee assistance program", and procedures for notifying employees of the plan's coverage and provisions.

Under 49 CFR 199.202, the alcohol misuse plan must contain methods and procedures for compliance with Subpart C, "including required testing, recordkeeping, reporting, education and training elements."
PHMSA or a certified State agency may, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing, require an operator to amend its plans to provide a reasonable level of safety (199.101(b)).

blocks.text: In practice, the plans are what an inspector reads first. Training content that does not match what the plans describe is a finding even if the content itself is sound, so plan and curriculum should be [mapped to each other](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations) and version controlled together.

sections.heading: What drug education must employees receive?

blocks.text: Every operator must provide an Employee Assistance Program (EAP) for its employees and for supervisors who make reasonable cause decisions, and each EAP must include education and training on drug use. [49 CFR 199.113](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-199.113) allows the EAP to be run in house or by contract and leaves rehabilitation to the operator's discretion.
Section 199.113(b) sets three minimum education elements:

items: Display and distribution of informational material.
Display and distribution of a community service hotline telephone number for employee assistance.
Display and distribution of the employer's policy regarding the use of prohibited drugs.

blocks.text: Part 199 does not set a minimum duration for employee education, unlike the 60 minute employee drug training in the transit rule covered in [FTA drug and alcohol training requirements](/regulations/fta-drug-and-alcohol-training-requirements). Operators still need records showing that each covered employee, including contractor staff, received the material.

sections.heading: What do the 199.113 and 199.241 supervisor training rules require?

blocks.text: Supervisors need one 60 minute period on drug use indicators and at least 60 minutes on alcohol misuse indicators. The drug module is part of the EAP in 199.113(c), and the alcohol module is a standalone rule in [49 CFR 199.241](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-199.241).

blocks.text: The alcohol testing rule in [49 CFR 199.225(b)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/199.225) explains why the training matters. The determination must rest on "specific, contemporaneous, articulable observations concerning the appearance, behavior, speech, or body odors of the employee", the observations must be made by a supervisor trained in detecting the symptoms of alcohol misuse, and the supervisor who makes the determination "shall not conduct the breath alcohol test on that employee."

Supervisors also need the timing rules: a record is required if the alcohol test is not given within 2 hours, attempts stop after 8 hours, and those records must be submitted to PHMSA on request. Even without a test, an employee showing behavioral, speech or performance indicators of alcohol misuse may not perform covered functions until a test shows less than 0.02 or the next regularly scheduled duty period begins, but not less than 8 hours after the determination.

sections.heading: How long must pipeline training records be kept?

blocks.text: Drug program training records are kept for at least three years and alcohol program training records for at least two years. The difference comes from two separate recordkeeping sections and is easy to miss when one system holds both.

items: [49 CFR 199.117(a)(4)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/199.117): records confirming that supervisors and employees have been trained as required by Part 199 are kept for at least 3 years, and training records must be made available to PHMSA or a State agency representative on request.

[49 CFR 199.227](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/199.227): alcohol program training records are kept for at least 2 years, and include alcohol misuse awareness materials with a copy of the alcohol policy, documentation of supervisor reasonable suspicion training, and certification that training complies with Subpart C.

blocks.text: A single three year retention rule for all drug and alcohol training evidence satisfies both minimums and is simpler to administer. See [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines the drug indicators, alcohol indicators, the bar on the deciding supervisor conducting the breath test and the 2 hour and 8 hour rules as separate knowledge points before content is written. Operators can then hold their own and contractor supervisors to the same assessed standard and keep evidence that suits both the 199.117 and 199.227 retention periods.

faqs.q: Does PHMSA require recurrent supervisor training?
faqs.a: No recurrent requirement is stated. As at November 2026, 49 CFR 199.113(c) requires one 60 minute period of drug training and 199.241 requires at least 60 minutes of alcohol training, with no refresher interval. Operators may set their own refresher cycle in their plans, which then becomes part of what inspectors check.

faqs.q: Do contractor supervisors need the PHMSA training?
faqs.a: If contractor supervisors make reasonable cause or reasonable suspicion determinations for covered employees, they need the training. Part 199 defines covered employees to include contractors and their employees, and the operator's plans must show how those determinations are made by trained people.

No. As at November 2026, 49 CFR 199.111 is reserved. The pipeline supervisor drug training requirement is in 49 CFR 199.113(c), within the Employee Assistance Program section, and the alcohol supervisor training requirement is in 49 CFR 199.241.

faqs.q: Does Part 199 apply to propane distribution systems?
faqs.a: Not to covered functions performed on pipeline systems that transport only petroleum gas or petroleum gas and air mixtures, or on master meter systems, under 49 CFR 199.2(c). Operators of other systems regulated under Parts 192, 193 or 195 are covered.
